claim: Mice fed a vitamin A-deficient diet exhibited lower abundances of serum amyloid A (Saa) 1 and 2 transcripts in the intestine as compared to mice fed a vitamin A-replete diet.
source: Microarray analysis disclosed that mice fed a vitamin A-deficient diet exhibited lower abundances of serum amyloid A (Saa) 1 and 2 transcripts in the intestine as compared to mice fed a vitamin A-replete diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 1

claim: Expression of small intestinal SAA1, 2, and 3 was reduced in mice fed a vitamin A-deficient diet.
source: Real-time quantitative PCR and immunofluorescence analysis verified that expression of small intestinal SAA1, 2, and 3 was reduced in mice fed a vitamin A-deficient diet (Figure 1A,B; Table 1).
evidence: Verified by Q-PCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Liver expression of SAA1 and 2 was reduced in mice fed a vitamin A-deficient diet.
source: Liver expression of SAA1 and 2 was also reduced in mice fed a vitamin A-deficient diet, although the reduction in expression was less pronounced than in the intestine (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by Q-PCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C,D

claim: Dietary vitamin A deficiency does not completely deplete stored retinoids in the liver.
source: This is likely because dietary vitamin A deficiency does not completely deplete stored retinoids in the liver (Liu and Gudas, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu and Gudas, 2005

claim: Elevated expression of intestinal Saa1 and Saa2 was observed following addition of retinol directly to the epithelial surface of small intestinal explants.
source: We also observed elevated expression of intestinal Saa1 and Saa2 following addition of retinol directly to the epithelial surface of small intestinal explants, and of liver Saa1 and Saa2 after intraperitoneal supplementation with retinoic acid (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Elevated expression of liver Saa1 and Saa2 was observed after intraperitoneal supplementation with retinoic acid.
source: We also observed elevated expression of intestinal Saa1 and Saa2 following addition of retinol directly to the epithelial surface of small intestinal explants, and of liver Saa1 and Saa2 after intraperitoneal supplementation with retinoic acid (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Addition of retinol or retinoic acid to cultured HepG2 cells enhanced expression of SAA1 and 2 in the presence of IL-1β and IL-6.
source: Addition of retinol or retinoic acid to cultured HepG2 cells (a human liver cell line) enhanced expression of SAA1 and 2 in the presence of IL-1β and IL-6 (Figure 1E,F)
evidence: Supported by cell culture data shown in Figure 1E,F

claim: The impact of dietary vitamin A on SAA expression is due to cell-intrinsic effects of retinoids.
source: Addition of retinol or retinoic acid to cultured HepG2 cells (a human liver cell line) enhanced expression of SAA1 and 2 in the presence of IL-1β and IL-6 (Figure 1E,F), suggesting that the impact of dietary vitamin A on SAA expression is due to cell-intrinsic effects of retinoids.
evidence: Inferred from HepG2 cell culture experiments showing direct effects of retinoids on SAA expression

claim: Full expression of SAAs in the intestine and liver requires dietary vitamin A.
source: Collectively, these results show that full expression of SAAs in the intestine and liver requires dietary vitamin A.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing reduced SAA expression in vitamin A-deficient conditions

claim: Retinol plays a vital role in the physiological response to microbial challenge.
source: Retinol plays a vital role in the physiological response to microbial challenge.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: Retinol can be converted enzymatically to retinoic acid, which complexes with nuclear receptors to regulate gene transcription programs in cells.
source: Retinol is derived from dietary vitamin A and can be converted enzymatically to retinoic acid, which complexes with nuclear receptors to regulate gene transcription programs in cells (Germain et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Germain et al., 2006

claim: Retinol promotes the maturation of innate immune cells.
source: In this way, retinol promotes the maturation of innate immune cells (Lawson and Berliner, 1999; Stephensen, 2001; Spencer et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawson and Berliner, 1999; Stephensen, 2001; Spencer et al., 2014

claim: Retinol governs the differentiation of adaptive immune cells.
source: In this way, retinol promotes the maturation of innate immune cells (Lawson and Berliner, 1999; Stephensen, 2001; Spencer et al., 2014), governs the differentiation of adaptive immune cells (Mucida et al., 2007; Hall et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mucida et al., 2007; Hall et al., 2011

claim: Retinol facilitates the regeneration of epithelial barriers damaged by infection.
source: In this way, retinol promotes the maturation of innate immune cells (Lawson and Berliner, 1999; Stephensen, 2001; Spencer et al., 2014), governs the differentiation of adaptive immune cells (Mucida et al., 2007; Hall et al., 2011), and facilitates the regeneration of epithelial barriers damaged by infection (Osanai et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Osanai et al., 2007

claim: A hallmark of vitamin A deficiency in humans is a markedly increased susceptibility to infection.
source: A hallmark of vitamin A deficiency in humans is a markedly increased susceptibility to infection (Sommer 2008, Underwood, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to Sommer 2008, Underwood, 2004

claim: Serum retinol binding protein (RBP) facilitates transport of retinol among the intestine, liver, and other tissues.
source: Serum retinol binding protein (RBP) facilitates transport of retinol among the intestine, which is the site of retinol acquisition, the liver, which is the major site of retinoid storage, and other tissues that require retinol for their physiological functions (Blaner, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blaner, 1989

claim: Serum RBP is markedly reduced following microbial challenge.
source: Despite the increased requirement for retinol, serum RBP is markedly reduced following microbial challenge (Rosales et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosales et al., 1996

claim: SAA proteins are expressed in the intestinal epithelium and liver and circulate in the serum.
source: Serum amyloid A (SAA) proteins are a family of proteins that are expressed in the intestinal epithelium (Eckhardt et al., 2010; Reigstad and Bäckhed, 2010) and liver (Uhlar and Whitehead, 1999) and circulate in the serum (Whitehead et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eckhardt et al., 2010; Reigstad and Bäckhed, 2010; Uhlar and Whitehead, 1999; Whitehead et al., 1992

claim: SAA family members are encoded in the genomes of virtually all vertebrates and are highly conserved among species.
source: SAA family members are encoded in the genomes of virtually all vertebrates and are highly conserved among species, suggesting essential biological functions (Uhlar et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uhlar et al., 1994

claim: Expression of SAAs is strongly induced by microbial exposure.
source: Expression of SAAs is strongly induced by microbial exposure.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with supporting citations in subsequent sentences

claim: SAAs are induced in intestinal epithelial cells by the microbiota.
source: SAAs are induced in intestinal epithelial cells by the microbiota (Ivanov et al., 2009; Reigstad et al., 2009; Eckhardt et al., 2010; Reigstad and Bäckhed, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Ivanov et al., 2009; Reigstad et al., 2009; Eckhardt et al., 2010; Reigstad and Bäckhed, 2010

claim: SAAs have been implicated in promoting Th17 cell development in response to specific microbiota components.
source: SAAs are induced in intestinal epithelial cells by the microbiota (Ivanov et al., 2009; Reigstad et al., 2009; Eckhardt et al., 2010; Reigstad and Bäckhed, 2010), and have been implicated in promoting Th17 cell development in response to specific microbiota components (Ivanov et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ivanov et al., 2009

claim: Liver and serum SAAs are markedly elevated following systemic bacterial or viral infection.
source: Similarly, liver and serum SAAs are markedly elevated following systemic bacterial or viral infection (Meek and Benditt, 1986; Chiba et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meek and Benditt, 1986; Chiba et al., 2009

claim: All SAAs are predicted to form amphipathic helices with a hydrophobic face that could interact with non-polar molecules.
source: First, all SAAs are predicted to form amphipathic helices with a hydrophobic face that could interact with non-polar molecules (Stevens, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stevens, 2004

claim: SAAs circulate in the serum associated with high-density lipoprotein (HDL).
source: Second, SAAs circulate in the serum associated with high-density lipoprotein (HDL), which transports lipid-bound lipoproteins amongst tissues (Whitehead et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitehead et al., 1992

claim: Mouse and human SAAs are retinol binding proteins.
source: Here, we show that mouse and human SAAs are retinol binding proteins.
evidence: Primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript

claim: SAA expression in mice requires dietary vitamin A.
source: We demonstrate that SAA expression in mice requires dietary vitamin A
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing reduced SAA expression in vitamin A-deficient mice

claim: Mouse and human SAAs bind tightly to retinol.
source: We demonstrate that SAA expression in mice requires dietary vitamin A, that mouse and human SAAs bind tightly to retinol
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorometric binding assays showing nanomolar affinity

claim: SAA recovered from serum following bacterial infection is associated with retinol.
source: We demonstrate that SAA expression in mice requires dietary vitamin A, that mouse and human SAAs bind tightly to retinol, and that SAA recovered from serum following bacterial infection is associated with retinol.
evidence: Demonstrated by LC-MS/MS analysis of SAA-enriched serum fractions

claim: Human SAA1 (hSAA1) bound retinol with an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 259 nM.
source: We did fluorometric titrations to determine apparent dissociation constants (Kds) for the all-trans isomer of retinol, and extracted Kds of 259, 169, and 145 nM for retinol binding to hSAA1, mSAA1, and mSAA3, respectively (Figure 2B,E).
evidence: Determined by fluorometric binding assays shown in Figure 2B,E

claim: Mouse SAA1 (mSAA1) bound retinol with an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 169 nM.
source: We did fluorometric titrations to determine apparent dissociation constants (Kds) for the all-trans isomer of retinol, and extracted Kds of 259, 169, and 145 nM for retinol binding to hSAA1, mSAA1, and mSAA3, respectively (Figure 2B,E).
evidence: Determined by fluorometric binding assays shown in Figure 2B,E

claim: Mouse SAA3 (mSAA3) bound retinol with an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 145 nM.
source: We did fluorometric titrations to determine apparent dissociation constants (Kds) for the all-trans isomer of retinol, and extracted Kds of 259, 169, and 145 nM for retinol binding to hSAA1, mSAA1, and mSAA3, respectively (Figure 2B,E).
evidence: Determined by fluorometric binding assays shown in Figure 2B,E

claim: The binding affinities of SAAs for retinol are similar to that of human serum retinol binding protein (hRBP).
source: These values are similar to binding affinities calculated for human serum retinol binding protein (hRBP) (Cogan et al., 1976) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison to hRBP binding affinity from Cogan et al., 1976 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Human SAA1 bound retinoic acid with a Kd of 268 nM.
source: Titration of all-trans retinoic acid yielded Kds of 268 and 224 nM for retinoic acid binding to hSAA1 and mSAA3, respectively (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: Determined by fluorescence quenching assays shown in Figure 2D,E

claim: Mouse SAA3 bound retinoic acid with a Kd of 224 nM.
source: Titration of all-trans retinoic acid yielded Kds of 268 and 224 nM for retinoic acid binding to hSAA1 and mSAA3, respectively (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: Determined by fluorescence quenching assays shown in Figure 2D,E

claim: There was weak binding of retinoic acid to mSAA1.
source: There was weak binding of retinoic acid to mSAA1 and we were unable to calculate a Kd for the interaction (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Observed in fluorescence quenching assays shown in Figure 2D,E

claim: hSAA1 and mSAA3 bind both retinol and retinoic acid, while mSAA1 selectively binds retinol.
source: Thus, while hSAA1 and mSAA3 bind both retinol and retinoic acid, mSAA1 selectively binds retinol.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from binding assay data showing differential binding patterns

claim: Human SAA1 bound β-carotene with a Kd of 497 nM.
source: mSAA1 also showed weak binding to other retinoids, including β-carotene and retinyl acetate, while hSAA1 bound these compounds with Kds of 497 and 347 nM, respectively, and mSAA3 bound β-carotene with a Kd of 159 nM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Determined by fluorescence quenching assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Human SAA1 bound retinyl acetate with a Kd of 347 nM.
source: mSAA1 also showed weak binding to other retinoids, including β-carotene and retinyl acetate, while hSAA1 bound these compounds with Kds of 497 and 347 nM, respectively, and mSAA3 bound β-carotene with a Kd of 159 nM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Determined by fluorescence quenching assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: Mouse SAA3 bound β-carotene with a Kd of 159 nM.
source: mSAA1 also showed weak binding to other retinoids, including β-carotene and retinyl acetate, while hSAA1 bound these compounds with Kds of 497 and 347 nM, respectively, and mSAA3 bound β-carotene with a Kd of 159 nM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Determined by fluorescence quenching assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: All SAA isoforms bound weakly to retinyl palmitate.
source: All SAA isoforms bound weakly to retinyl palmitate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Observed in fluorescence quenching assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: Long chain retinyl esters (such as retinyl palmitate) are the major form of stored retinoid in the liver.
source: Since long chain retinyl esters (such as retinyl palmitate) are the major form of stored retinoid in the liver (Vogel et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Vogel et al., 1999

claim: SAAs do not transport retinoids for storage.
source: Since long chain retinyl esters (such as retinyl palmitate) are the major form of stored retinoid in the liver (Vogel et al., 1999), this suggests that SAAs do not transport retinoids for storage.
evidence: Inferred from weak binding of SAAs to retinyl palmitate

claim: Cholesterol was unable to competitively inhibit retinol binding to SAAs.
source: Although a role for SAAs in cholesterol transport and metabolism has been proposed (van der Westhuyzen et al., 2005), we found that cholesterol was unable to competitively inhibit retinol binding to SAAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by competitive inhibition assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D

claim: SAAs constitute a high proportion of serum protein during acute systemic infection.
source: However, SAAs constitute a high proportion of serum protein during acute systemic infection (McAdam and Sipe, 1976; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to McAdam and Sipe, 1976; Zhang et al., 2005

claim: Size exclusion chromatography was used to recover a SAA-enriched fraction from the sera of mice infected intraperitoneally with Salmonella typhimurium for 24 hr.
source: We were therefore able to use size exclusion chromatography to recover a SAA-enriched fraction from the sera of mice infected intraperitoneally with Salmonella typhimurium for 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Described method with results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: The SAA-enriched protein fraction was devoid of other known retinol binding proteins.
source: Mass spectrometry revealed that the SAA-enriched protein fraction was devoid of other known retinol binding proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Determined by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) indicated the presence of retinol in the SAA-enriched fraction.
source: Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) indicated the presence of retinol in the SAA-enriched fraction (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C)
evidence: Determined by LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: The molar ratio of retinol to SAA in the SAA-enriched fraction was approximately 1 mol retinol per 4 mol SAA.
source: Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) indicated the presence of retinol in the SAA-enriched fraction (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C) in a molar ratio of ∼1 mol retinol/4 mol SAA (Figure 3, inset).
evidence: Calculated from LC-MS/MS and Western blot quantification shown in Figure 3 inset

claim: Retinoic acid was not detected in the SAA-enriched fraction.
source: In these analyses, retinoic acid was not detected, and retinol was not detected in the equivalent serum fraction recovered from Saa1/2−/− mice (Eckhardt et al., 2010) (Figure 3)
evidence: Determined by LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: Retinol was not detected in the equivalent serum fraction recovered from Saa1/2−/− mice.
source: In these analyses, retinoic acid was not detected, and retinol was not detected in the equivalent serum fraction recovered from Saa1/2−/− mice (Eckhardt et al., 2010) (Figure 3)
evidence: Determined by LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: The retinol detected in serum fractions was preferentially associated with SAA.
source: In these analyses, retinoic acid was not detected, and retinol was not detected in the equivalent serum fraction recovered from Saa1/2−/− mice (Eckhardt et al., 2010) (Figure 3), suggesting that the retinol was preferentially associated with SAA.
evidence: Inferred from absence of retinol in Saa1/2−/− mice and absence of other retinol binding proteins

claim: SAAs lack sequence homology to the two known families of retinol binding proteins: cellular retinol binding proteins (CRBP) and serum retinol binding proteins (RBP).
source: SAAs lack sequence homology to the two known families of retinol binding proteins: cellular retinol binding proteins (CRBP) and serum retinol binding proteins (RBP) (Blaner, 1989; Noy, 2000).
evidence: Stated as fact with supporting citations to Blaner, 1989; Noy, 2000

claim: The three-dimensional structure of recombinant mSAA3 was determined by X-ray crystallography.
source: To understand how SAAs bind retinol, we therefore determined the three-dimensional structure of recombinant mSAA3 by X-ray crystallography.
evidence: Described method with results shown in Figure 4 and Table 2

claim: The mSAA3 protein was crystallized in a P62 space group with two subunits in the asymmetric unit.
source: The protein was crystallized in a P62 space group with two subunits in the asymmetric unit, and the structure was determined to a resolution of 2 Å by single-wavelength anomalous dispersion (SAD) phasing using a selenomethionyl-derivatived crystal (Figure 4A; Table 2).
evidence: Crystallographic data shown in Figure 4A and Table 2

claim: The mSAA3 structure was determined to a resolution of 2 Å by single-wavelength anomalous dispersion (SAD) phasing using a selenomethionyl-derivatived crystal.
source: The protein was crystallized in a P62 space group with two subunits in the asymmetric unit, and the structure was determined to a resolution of 2 Å by single-wavelength anomalous dispersion (SAD) phasing using a selenomethionyl-derivatived crystal (Figure 4A; Table 2).
evidence: Crystallographic data shown in Figure 4A and Table 2

claim: The crystal structure reveals that mSAA3 is highly α-helical.
source: The crystal structure reveals that mSAA3 is highly α-helical (Figure 4A), as predicted on the basis of its primary sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Stevens, 2004).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 4A

claim: The mSAA3 structure is very similar to the recently determined structure of human SAA1.1.
source: The structure is very similar to the recently determined structure of human SAA1.1 (Lu et al., 2014), an isoform that has a marked tendency to form pathogenic amyloid fibrils (Yu et al., 2000).
evidence: Comparison to structure from Lu et al., 2014

claim: The mSAA3 structure consists of four α-helices, designated α1-4 from the N- to the C-termini, forming a cone-shaped four-helix bundle.
source: Like the SAA1.1 structure, the mSAA3 structure consists of four α-helices, designated α1-4 from the N- to the C-termini, forming a cone-shaped four-helix bundle with a comparatively longer α1.
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 4A

claim: The helices in mSAA3 form two sets of antiparallel helices, α1-α2 and α3-α4, connected by a very short loop.
source: The helices form two sets of antiparallel helices, α1-α2 and α3-α4, connected by a very short loop (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 4A

claim: The mSAA3 monomer is stabilized by an extensive network of hydrogen bonding interactions among conserved residues and water molecules in the interior of the monomer.
source: The monomer is stabilized by an extensive network of hydrogen bonding interactions among conserved residues and water molecules in the interior of the monomer.
evidence: Observed in crystal structure analysis

claim: The C-terminal tail of mSAA3 wraps around the helix bundle making a number of hydrogen bonding interactions that add to monomer stability.
source: As in the SAA1.1 structure, the C-terminal tail wraps around the helix bundle making a number of hydrogen bonding interactions that add to monomer stability, underscoring the importance of the C-terminal tail.
evidence: Observed in crystal structure, comparison to SAA1.1 structure

claim: Size exclusion chromatography showed that mSAA3 forms a tetramer in solution.
source: Size exclusion chromatography and cross-linking experiments showed that mSAA3 forms a tetramer in solution (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography and cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: Cross-linking experiments showed that mSAA3 forms a tetramer in solution.
source: Size exclusion chromatography and cross-linking experiments showed that mSAA3 forms a tetramer in solution (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by size exclusion chromatography and cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: Analysis of the mSAA3 crystal structure using the Protein Interfaces, Surfaces and Assemblies (PDBePISA) server yielded a tetrameric quaternary structure.
source: Consistent with these findings, analysis of the mSAA3 crystal structure using the Protein Interfaces, Surfaces and Assemblies (PDBePISA) server (http://www.ebi.ac.uk/msd-srv/prot_int/) yielded a tetrameric quaternary structure (Figure 4B; Table 3).
evidence: Computational analysis of crystal structure shown in Figure 4B and Table 3

claim: The mSAA3 tetrameric structure is in contrast to the hexameric structure derived for SAA1.1.
source: This is in contrast to the hexameric structure derived for SAA1.1 (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to structure from Lu et al., 2014

claim: Different SAAs can adopt different oligomeric states.
source: First, it has been suggested that different SAAs can adopt different oligomeric states (Wang et al., 2002, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2002, 2011

claim: SAA1.1 was observed to produce a ∼43 kDa species in solution.
source: SAA1.1 was also observed to produce a ∼43 kDa species in solution (Lu et al., 2014), suggesting that SAA1.1 may in part adopt a tetrameric state.
evidence: Observation from Lu et al., 2014

claim: SAA1.1 has a more hydrophobic N-terminus than mSAA3, which is thought to be a determinant of amyloidogenicity.
source: Second, SAA1.1 has a more hydrophobic N-terminus than mSAA3, which is thought to be a determinant of amyloidogenicity (Yu et al., 2000; Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yu et al., 2000; Lu et al., 2014

claim: The mSAA3 tetramer is formed by two sets of tightly associated dimers.
source: The mSAA3 tetramer is formed by two sets of tightly associated dimers (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 4B,C

claim: The dimers in mSAA3 pack against each other through an aromatic interface formed by W71, as well as a non-polar interaction involving V75 residues.
source: The dimers pack against each other through an aromatic interface formed by W71, as well as a non-polar interaction involving V75 residues (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 4C,E

claim: The dimer in mSAA3 is formed by two identical chains oriented pseudo-anti-parallel to each other.
source: The dimer is formed by two identical chains oriented pseudo-anti-parallel to each other, and is held together by two pairs of tight hydrogen bond interactions between K74 and D78 residues on oppositely oriented α3 helices (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: The dimer in mSAA3 is held together by two pairs of tight hydrogen bond interactions between K74 and D78 residues on oppositely oriented α3 helices.
source: The dimer is formed by two identical chains oriented pseudo-anti-parallel to each other, and is held together by two pairs of tight hydrogen bond interactions between K74 and D78 residues on oppositely oriented α3 helices (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: The dimer interaction in mSAA3 is supported by a set of aromatic interactions between F99 and W103 of the α4 helices.
source: The interaction is also supported by a set of aromatic interactions between F99 and W103 of the α4 helices (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: The interactions in mSAA3 result in tightly held α3 helices composed primarily of non-polar residues, thus forming the inside hollow pocket of the tetramer.
source: These interactions result in tightly held α3 helices composed primarily of non-polar residues, thus forming the inside hollow pocket of the tetramer.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis of crystal structure

claim: The hollow pocket in mSAA3 is surrounded by the remaining helices, creating a hydrophobic interior that is protected from the external aqueous environment.
source: The hollow pocket is surrounded by the remaining helices, creating a hydrophobic interior that is protected from the external aqueous environment.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis of crystal structure

claim: Retinol is a highly apolar lipid-like molecule consisting of a β-ionone ring, an isoprenoid tail, and a hydroxyl group.
source: Retinol is a highly apolar lipid-like molecule consisting of a β-ionone ring, an isoprenoid tail, and a hydroxyl group.
evidence: Stated as established chemical knowledge

claim: Retinol requires a non-polar environment for transport among tissues and within cells.
source: Thus, it requires a non-polar environment for transport among tissues and within cells.
evidence: Inferred from the apolar nature of retinol

claim: Known retinol binding proteins consist mainly of β-sheet secondary structures forming a β-barrel tertiary structure, with the retinol molecule held in an interior non-polar binding pocket.
source: Structures of known retinol binding proteins, including serum RBP, indicate that these proteins consist mainly of β-sheet secondary structures forming a β-barrel tertiary structure, with the retinol molecule held in an interior non-polar binding pocket (Newcomer et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to Newcomer et al., 1984

claim: mSAA3 is α-helical and oligomerizes to form a hollow, largely non-polar interior that could serve as a binding pocket for a non-polar small molecule.
source: In contrast, mSAA3 is α-helical and oligomerizes to form a hollow, largely non-polar interior that could serve as a binding pocket for a non-polar small molecule (Figure 6A).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 6A

claim: A ligand docking analysis using SwissDock indicated that retinol can be docked in the mSAA3 hydrophobic pocket with favorable free energy (∼ −7 kcal/mol) and FullFitness values (∼ −2400 kcal/mol).
source: However, a ligand docking analysis using SwissDock (Grosdidier et al., 2011) indicated that retinol can be docked in this hydrophobic pocket with favorable free energy (∼ −7 kcal/mol) and FullFitness values (Zoete et al., 2010) (∼ −2400 kcal/mol) (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Computational docking analysis shown in Figure 6B–D

claim: Introducing a Trp71Ala (W71A) mutation in the mSAA3 hydrophobic core reduced the affinity of mSAA3 for retinol.
source: Consistent with this prediction, introducing a Trp71Ala (W71A) mutation in the mSAA3 hydrophobic core reduced the affinity of mSAA3 for retinol (Figure 6E).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorometric binding assays of mutant protein shown in Figure 6E

claim: The mSAA3 structure supports the biochemical data showing a retinol binding function for SAAs.
source: Thus, the mSAA3 structure supports our biochemical data showing a retinol binding function for SAAs and explains how mSAA3 could bind retinol.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from integration of structural and biochemical data

claim: SAAs are strongly induced by microbial exposure at sites of retinol uptake (intestine) and storage (liver), and are present at high levels in the circulation following microbial challenge.
source: First, SAAs are strongly induced by microbial exposure at sites of retinol uptake (intestine) and storage (liver), and are present at high levels in the circulation following microbial challenge (Chiba et al., 2009; Ivanov et al., 2009; Reigstad et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chiba et al., 2009; Ivanov et al., 2009; Reigstad et al., 2009

claim: SAAs bind retinol at nanomolar affinity in vitro.
source: Second, we have shown that SAAs bind retinol at nanomolar affinity in vitro, and that serum SAAs circulate in association with retinol.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorometric binding assays in the study

claim: Serum SAAs circulate in association with retinol.
source: Second, we have shown that SAAs bind retinol at nanomolar affinity in vitro, and that serum SAAs circulate in association with retinol.
evidence: Demonstrated by LC-MS/MS analysis of serum fractions in the study

claim: The three dimensional structure of mSAA3 exhibits a hollow hydrophobic binding pocket.
source: Third, the three dimensional structure of mSAA3 exhibits a hollow hydrophobic binding pocket, providing structural insight into how SAAs bind retinol.
evidence: Demonstrated by crystal structure determination in the study

claim: Saa1/2−/− mice exhibit increased susceptibility to chemically-induced colitis.
source: First, Saa1/2−/− mice exhibit increased susceptibility to chemically-induced colitis in mice (Eckhardt et al., 2010), suggesting that SAAs contribute to intestinal immunity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Eckhardt et al., 2010

claim: Commensal microbiota stimulate neutrophil migration through induction of SAA in zebrafish.
source: Second, studies in zebrafish show that commensal microbiota stimulate neutrophil migration through induction of SAA (Kanther et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanther et al., 2013

claim: Intraperitoneal infection of Saa1/2−/− mice with S. typhimurium resulted in higher bacterial loads in liver and spleen as compared to wild-type mice.
source: Third, we found that intraperitoneal infection of Saa1/2−/− mice with S. typhimurium resulted in higher bacterial loads in liver and spleen as compared to wild-type mice (Figure 7A,B), suggesting that SAAs also contribute to systemic immunity.
